clue.text: Crimes committed with collusion behind bars, damaging pieces of work

blocks.note: someone behind bars is inside, in prison
pieces of work are jobs, and in criminal slang a job is a damaging one such as a robbery

explanation.surface: A gang of prisoners plotting together to wreck the work they are set inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind bars' reads as part of the crime story but simply supplies the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: An inside job is a crime carried out with help from someone within the targeted organisation.

clue.text: Disliking work, I must get led astray

indicators.note: something led astray wanders off its proper course, so the letters wander out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
the three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone confessing that, as a shirker, they are bound to be tempted into bad ways.
explanation.definitionFit: An idle person is lazy, averse to doing any labour.

clue.text: Seeing that about open

blocks.note: 'seeing that' and 'since' both mean 'because'
re means concerning, about

explanation.surface: A fragment of reasoning: given that something is roughly open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like it should wrap something, but here it is just the short word meaning concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: Open and sincere both describe someone honest and frank, without hidden motives.

clue.text: Lies stranded, unfortunately, in remote spot

indicators.note: things that go unfortunately go wrong, so these letters come out in the wrong order

blocks.note: the twelve letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A castaway lies stranded, sadly, somewhere far from anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface itself describes being marooned, so the anagram fodder doubles as a picture of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert island is an uninhabited isle far from civilisation, the classic isolated place.

clue.text: Lexicographer producing Gospel, very new

blocks.note: John is one of the four Gospels
so means very, as in 'so good'
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A dictionary-maker publishing a fresh version of the Gospels.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Johnson compiled the famous 1755 Dictionary of the English Language.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Samuel Johnson is the best-known English compiler of dictionaries, an example of the type.

clue.text: Fruit bats

blocks.note: first meaning: the yellow tropical fruit, in the plural
second meaning: crazy, as in 'gone nuts'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit bats' reads as the flying mammal; split it, and 'bats' is the informal adjective for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Bananas are a fruit, and 'bananas' is also slang for mad, just as 'bats' is.

clue.text: Mark causing alarm, no end

indicators.note: having no end means the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a scare is something that causes alarm

explanation.surface: A frightening blemish that seems to go on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is the lasting mark left on skin after a wound heals.

clue.text: Insincere talk in a rural Mexican bar

blocks.note: cant is hypocritical, pious talk
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Empty chatter heard in a country drinking spot south of the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a' looks like a link telling us where the talk happens, but both words go straight into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantina is a Spanish-American tavern or bar, typical of small towns and villages.

clue.text: Official car leaving property

blocks.note: real in the sense of genuine, recognised, official
an estate is a British name for a station wagon

explanation.surface: A government car driving away from a building.
explanation.walkthrough: An estate car is the British term for a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: Real estate is land and buildings, i.e. property in the legal sense.

clue.text: Helps a farm labourer after loans

indicators.note: after places the labourer behind the loans word in the answer

blocks.note: to loan is to lend
a hand is a farm worker

explanation.surface: A farm worker taken on once the bank has given credit.
explanation.definitionFit: To lend a hand is the idiom for giving assistance.

clue.text: Indian's home, Central America

blocks.note: at home means in
the initials of Central America

explanation.surface: Where a Native American lives: Central America.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay rather than showing possession.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca were an indigenous people of South America, so an Inca is an American Indian.

clue.text: Cook so keen to make a flan

blocks.note: to bake is to cook in an oven
'well' and 'so' are both conversational openers
keen and tart both mean sharp

explanation.surface: A cook so enthusiastic they set about producing a flan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' reads as eager but means sharp or acid here. A Bakewell tart is an English almond and jam pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bakewell tart is an open pastry case with a filling, the kind of dish called a flan.

clue.text: Typical member of parliament, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: characteristic of a class, as an adjective
second meaning: an elected person who acts for constituents, 'perhaps' marking an example

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase about an ordinary politician, but the first word is a definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A representative sample is a typical one; an MP is an elected spokesperson for voters.

clue.text: Foolish male, fellow crossing one place in field

indicators.note: crossing one is read as straddling it, so the male fellow pair goes around the single letter

blocks.note: silly means foolish
M is the abbreviation for male
a don is a university fellow
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A silly man walking across a field.
explanation.walkthrough: Silly mid-on is a cricket fielding position close to the batsman on the leg side; 'silly' in cricket means dangerously near.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the fielders stand at named spots, and silly mid-on is one such position on the field.

clue.text: A Spaniard, and native of one African country, heading off

indicators.note: with its heading gone, the first letter is removed

blocks.note: a person from Liberia in West Africa

explanation.surface: A Spaniard and an African setting off together.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain occupies most of the Iberian peninsula, so a Spaniard is an Iberian.

clue.text: Racing driver we upset during launch

indicators.note: upset in a down-or-across sense means turned over, so the short word is read back to front
during places one thing within the time span of another, so it sits inside

blocks.note: a launch is a start
the pronoun turned round

explanation.surface: A racing driver and team got upset at the start of the race.
explanation.walkthrough: Jackie Stewart was a Scottish Formula One world champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Jackie Stewart won three Formula One titles, a famous example of a motor-racing driver.

clue.text: Girl with mate back on one of the Canary Islands

indicators.note: back means going in the opposite direction, so the friend word is read from the right

blocks.note: a pal is a mate, a friend
Alma is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl and her partner returning from a holiday island.
explanation.definitionFit: La Palma is a volcanic island in the Canaries archipelago, off north-west Africa.

clue.text: Faint in narrow defile abroad

blocks.note: a pass is a narrow route through mountains
out means away, abroad

explanation.surface: Someone collapsing while trekking a mountain gorge overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass out is the idiom for losing consciousness, i.e. to faint.

clue.text: Jumping bail, seaman, a pantomime hero

indicators.note: jumping about suggests letters leaping out of place

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor skipping bail, then turning up as the hero of a Christmas show.
explanation.walkthrough: Pantomime is a British Christmas stage show based on fairy tales; Ali Baba is a stock pantomime story.
explanation.definitionFit: Ali Baba, of the forty thieves, is the title character of a traditional British pantomime.

clue.text: Clown making most of mistake in part of theatre

indicators.note: most of means everything except the last letter
in means placed inside the theatre word

blocks.note: the pit is the area where the orchestra or cheap seats are
a mistake is an error

explanation.surface: A clown blundering on stage for most of the show.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierrot is the sad white-faced clown of French pantomime and commedia tradition.

clue.text: Papers supporting professional image

indicators.note: in a down answer, supporting means sitting underneath, so the papers come after the professional

blocks.note: pro is short for professional
a file is a set of papers

explanation.surface: Documents backing up an expert's public image.
explanation.definitionFit: A profile is the public impression or image someone presents.

clue.text: Rating showed card

blocks.note: ran as in a cinema ran a film, i.e. showed it
the king is a playing card

explanation.surface: A grade given for a scorecard that was shown.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranking is a position on a scale, the same as a rating.

clue.text: Lawyer Perry and policeman George on course for state boundary

blocks.note: Perry Mason is the fictional TV defence lawyer
George Dixon is the bobby of the British TV series Dixon of Dock Green
a line is a course or route

explanation.surface: A TV lawyer and a TV policeman heading off on a trip to a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: Dixon of Dock Green was a long-running British police drama about a London constable.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mason-Dixon line is the surveyed border between Pennsylvania and Maryland, dividing US states.

clue.text: Ringo, short celebrity

indicators.note: cut short means the final letter is lopped off

blocks.note: Ringo Starr was the Beatles' drummer

explanation.surface: The Beatles drummer, a famous little man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like a remark on Ringo's height, but it trims his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A star is a famous performer, a celebrity.

clue.text: Crucifix over entrance

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the word runs the other way

blocks.note: a rood is a cross or crucifix in a church

explanation.surface: A crucifix hung above a church entrance.
explanation.definitionFit: A door is the way in, an entrance to a building or room.

clue.text: Free enterprise supporter in Moscow, say, is tense

blocks.note: Moscow is an example of a capital city
taken as written
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A market economist in Russia's capital feels nervous.
explanation.definitionFit: A capitalist backs a private-ownership market economy, the free enterprise system.

clue.text: Pay close attention to college turning

indicators.note: turning round makes the word face the other way

blocks.note: Eton is the famous English public school, Eton College

explanation.surface: Advice to watch a school as it changes direction.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton College is an elite English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: To note something is to observe it carefully and take heed.

clue.text: Daily row about Germany's leader, not a real threat

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
about means going around, so the row word surrounds

blocks.note: a daily is a newspaper
a tier is a row, as of seats
the first letter of the country name

explanation.surface: A newspaper quarrel over the German chancellor, which turns out to be harmless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel, but it is a line of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper tiger is something that appears menacing but is actually ineffectual.
